That is a great book to start with. It has not yet been updated for C++11/14/17, but it's still relevant and worth reading.

This list on Stack Overflow is the best answer to "where do I start learning C++" that I'm aware of: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/388242/the-definitive-c-book-guide-and-list

Sticking to books is generally the recommended route for learning C++. There is a lot of online material out there, but it's hard to know whether it's good quality or not. C++ has been around for a long time now. As such, lots of people have written lots about it. The problem is that people tend to be eager to share their knowledge, and often do so without a correct understanding of what they are writing about. C++ especially suffers from this due its age (more content has been produced over time), popularity (more people want to write about it), and complexity. It is quite easy to misunderstand something in the language without realizing it, as oftentimes things will appear to work as expected even when they are actually ill-formed.

Regarding your second question, I'm guessing that "xxxx" most often refers to a compiler option. These are specific to the compiler you are using, but you're somewhat abstracted away from them if you are using CMake, since CMake generates the files that in turn are used to drive the compiler. You will probably have to work backwards from someone saying "compile with -std=c++11" to determine what you need to do with CMake to generate a Makefile that results in compilation with that option. I haven't spent any time with CLion yet, so there may be other nuances involved in how it drives the compiler.

I would suggest taking the time to learn how to work directly with the compiler without aid of an IDE. IDEs are great, but understanding how to work with just the compiler and linker and understanding that the IDE is not a compiler (a lot of Visual Studio users seem to fall into this trap) and that IDE settings like "Debug" and "Release" modes have no intrinsic meaning will be a big help to you down the road. Being able to isolate some code you are having trouble with into a single file that you can pass to the compiler directly is a hugely useful skill that many people I encounter haven't learned yet.

What are the Classics?

From Wikipedia:

Classics (also Classical Studies) is the study of the languages, literature, laws, philosophy, history, art, archaeology and other material culture of Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome; especially during Classical Antiquity (ca. BCE 600 – AD 600). Traditionally, the study of Classical literature (Greek and Roman) was the principal study of the humanities.

Put simply, Classics is the study of the world of Ancient Greece and Rome. Those who study the subject are known as 'Classicists'.

Don't be afraid to post just because you aren't an authority on the subject. No classicist is an expert on all matters Greco-Roman. We're all here to learn, to educate, or discuss. Or maybe we just came for pretty pictures of the Parthenon.
